title: To catch a king
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: Anna Keay reviews Charles Spencer’s book about the hunt for King Charles II
during the English Civil War of the seventeenth century

Charles Spencer’s latest book, To Catch a King, tells us the story of the hunt for King Charles II in the six weeks after his resounding defeat at the Battle of Worcester in September 1651. And what a story it is. After his father was executed by the Parliamentarians in 1649, the young Charles II sacrificed one of the very principles his father had died for and did a deal with the Scots, thereby accepting Presbyterianism* as the national religion in return for being crowned King of Scots. His arrival in Edinburgh prompted the English Parliamentary army to invade Scotland in a pre-emptive strike. This was followed by a Scottish invasion of England. The two sides finally faced one another at Worcester in the west of England in 1651. After being comprehensively defeated on the meadows outside the city by the Parliamentarian army, the 21-year-old king found himself the subject of a national manhunt, with a huge sum offered for his capture. Over the following six weeks he managed, through a series of heart-poundingly close escapes, to evade the Parliamentarians before seeking refuge in France. For the next nine years, the penniless and defeated Charles wandered around Europe with only a small group of loyal supporters.

Years later, after his restoration as king, the 50-year-old Charles II requested a meeting with the writer and diarist Samuel Pepys. His intention when asking Pepys to commit his story to paper was to ensure that this most extraordinary episode was never forgotten. Over two three-hour sittings, the king related to him in great detail his personal recollections of the six weeks he had spent as a fugitive. As the king and secretary settled down (a scene that is surely a gift for a future scriptwriter), Charles commenced his story: ‘After the battle was so absolutely lost as to be beyond hope of recovery, I began to think of the best way of saving myself.’

One of the joys of Spencer’s book, a result not least of its use of Charles II’s own narrative as well as those of his supporters, is just how close the reader gets to the action. The day-byday retelling of the fugitives’ doings provides delicious details: the cutting of the king’s long hair with agricultural shears, the use of walnut leaves to dye his pale skin, and the day Charles spent lying on a branch of the great oak tree in Boscobel Wood as the Parliamentary soldiers scoured the forest floor below. Spencer draws out both the humour – such as the preposterous refusal of Charles’s friend Henry Wilmot to adopt disguise on the grounds that it was beneath his dignity – and the emotional tension when the secret of the king’s presence was cautiously revealed to his supporters.

Charles’s adventures after losing the Battle of Worcester hide the uncomfortable truth that whilst almost everyone in England had been appalled by the execution of his father, they had not welcomed the arrival of his son with the Scots army, but had instead firmly bolted their doors. This was partly because he rode at the head of what looked like a foreign invasion force and partly because, after almost a decade of civil war, people were desperate to avoid it beginning again. This makes it all the more interesting that Charles II himself loved the story so much ever after. As well as retelling it to anyone who would listen, causing eyerolling among courtiers, he set in train a series of initiatives to memorialise it. There was to be a new order of chivalry, the Knights of the Royal Oak. A series of enormous oil paintings depicting the episode were produced, including a two-metre-wide canvas of Boscobel Wood and a set of six similarly enormous paintings of the king on the run. In 1660, Charles II commissioned the artist John Michael Wright to paint a flying squadron of cherubs* carrying an oak tree to the heavens on the ceiling of his bedchamber. It is hard to imagine many other kings marking the lowest point in their life so enthusiastically, or indeed pulling off such an escape in the first place.

Charles Spencer is the perfect person to pass the story on to a new generation. His pacey, readable prose steers deftly clear of modern idioms and elegantly brings to life the details of the great tale. He has even-handed sympathy for both the fugitive king and the fierce republican regime that hunted him, and he succeeds in his desire to explore far more of the background of the story than previous books on the subject have done. Indeed, the opening third of the book is about how Charles II found himself at Worcester in the first place, which for some will be reason alone to read To Catch a King.

The tantalising question left, in the end, is that of what it all meant. Would Charles II have been a different king had these six weeks never happened? The days and nights spent in hiding must have affected him in some way. Did the need to assume disguises, to survive on wit and charm alone, to use trickery and subterfuge to escape from tight corners help form him? This is the one area where the book doesn’t quite hit the mark. Instead its depiction of Charles II in his final years as an ineffective, pleasure-loving monarch doesn’t do justice to the man (neither is it accurate), or to the complexity of his character. But this one niggle aside, To Catch a King is an excellent read, and those who come to it knowing little of the famous tale will find they have a treat in store.
* cherub: an image of angelic children used in paintings

groups.contextHtml:
The story behind the hunt for Charles II


Charles II’s father was executed by the Parliamentarian forces in 1649. Charles II then formed a [27] ______  with the Scots, and in order to become King of Scots, he abandoned an important [28] ______  that was held by his father and had contributed to his father’s death. The opposing sides then met outside Worcester in 1651. The battle led to a [29] ______  for the Parliamentarians and Charles had to flee for his life. A [30] ______  was offered for Charles’s capture, but after six weeks spent in hiding, he eventually managed to reach the [31] ______ of continental Europe.

groups.instruction:
Questions 32–35

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

Choose

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer

NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer

NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.prompt: Charles chose Pepys for the task because he considered him to be trustworthy.
questions.explanation: 本题的定位可以说是难也不难：不难在于凭借大写人名Pepys即可快速定位到第二段的第一句话；难则在于无论是这句话本身还是后文的若干句话，都只是客观记述了查理指派Pepys来写自己流亡故事的经过，并没有给出查理之所以选择他的具体理由。因此，追求准确答题的考生需要将本题的定位与接下来的33题结合起来进行，在已经明确找到33题原文定位而依然没有发现本题的对应信息时，才能有更大的把握确认答案为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: Charles’s personal recollection of the escape lacked sufficient detail.
questions.explanation: 本题可以直接凭借原词重现的personal recollection在原文中找到答案出处句，且句意表述非常直白，明确提出国王的讲述方式是in great detail，与题干所说的lack sufficient detail形成了直接的矛盾抵触，考生可轻松得出答案为NO。

questions.prompt: Charles indicated to Pepys that he had planned his escape before the battle.
questions.explanation: 本题的出处与前两道题非常接近，都是Pepys接受委托开始著书的故事情节，考生不妨由此得到提示，在阅读第二段每一句话时耐心看懂文意，应该就不会错过定位句的信息。文中用直接引语的方式表达了查理本人的说法：是在战事已经一败涂地之后他才开始思考自救方式的，这与题干的时间节点形成了直接矛盾，由此可得出答案为NO。

questions.prompt: The inclusion of Charles’s account is a positive aspect of the book.
questions.explanation: 本题的出处与前三道题接近，且无论是题干中的account还是对应原文中的narrative，都不是难度高的认知词汇，考生应该可以比较容易地找到出处。原文中再次出现了本套试题第一篇文章中重点讲解过的not least。该词组的字面意思“并非最少”略显别扭，实则表达的意思是“相当重要”，可见文章专门强调了查理本人的自述是本书阅读乐趣的一个重要来源，这与题干的表述意思相符，因此答案为YES。

groups.instruction:
Questions 36–40

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's main purpose in the first paragraph?

options.text: to describe what happened during the Battle of Worcester
to give an account of the circumstances leading to Charles II's escape
to provide details of the Parliamentarians' political views
to compare Charles II's beliefs with those of his father

questions.explanation:
虽然问题句已经明确告知考生答案出处在第一段，但这种情况下的绝大多数正确答案都不是依靠只读段落中的某一句话就能锁定的；因此，考生不如一开始就抱定平行阅读的思路，直接从第一句话顺序读下来，获得对本段大意和叙事逻辑的正确理解。首句开门见山地点明这本书的主要内容，第二句马上跟进，夸赞这故事真不错。接下来，后面的句子依次按照史实顺序列出了查理二世从放弃自己父王的宗教信仰而转投其他教派、以此换取加冕为王，到前往苏格兰引发议会军先发制人发动袭击，再到苏格兰军队反攻、双方遭遇激战后查理惨败，最后查理经历惊魂六周的东躲西藏后流亡欧洲。即使不考虑所有的细节描述，考生也应当不难看出这是在讲述一系列导致查理二世最终逃亡海外的历史事件发展，从而确定正确答案应为B项：to give an account of the circumstances leading to Charles II’s escape（讲述最终导致了查理二世逃亡的一系列事件）。

A项：to describe what happened during the Battle of Worcester

译文：描绘在Worcester战役中都发生了什么

虽然这场战役的名称确实作为细节信息之一出现在了第一段里，但却不足以代表整段大意，更是无法涵盖故事的全貌。

C项：to provide details of the Parliamentarians’ political views

译文：为议会军的政治主张提供细节说明

这个选项与B项类似，只是采用了在本段中确实出现不止一次的“议会军”这个名称，但却不是段落总体篇幅中想要表达的主题或大意。

D项：to compare Charles II’s beliefs with those of his father

译文：比较查理二世与其父王的不同信念信仰

看过第一段后读者不难看出，查理二世确实接受了与其父王所不同的宗教信仰，然而这一点并不是第一段的主要内容，当然也不是书评者在第一段里着墨最多的部分。综合来看，三个混淆选项的辨识排除难度都不高，因为都仅仅只是表面借用了段落中的某个细节单词或信息而已，考生只要稍加注意就不难做出正确选择。

questions.prompt: Why does the reviewer include examples of the fugitives' behaviour in the third paragraph?

options.text: to explain how close Charles II came to losing his life
to suggest that Charles II's supporters were badly prepared
to illustrate how the events of the six weeks are brought to life
to argue that certain aspects are not as well known as they should be

questions.explanation:
第三段的第一句话已经点明：Spencer所著这本书的阅读乐趣之一正是在于里面包含了查理本人及其支持者的亲口讲述，从而让读者更身临其境地看到了事件发展过程。接下来段落的所有篇幅都用举例说明来支持第一句话提出的主张，这样一来，对比几个选项的意思，考生应该就不难顺利选出正确答案为C项：to illustrate how the events of the six weeks are brought to life（为了证明这六周的事件是如何被栩栩如生地展示出来的）。

A项：to explain how close Charles II came to losing his life

译文：为了解释查理二世如何差一点儿就丧了命

从本段内容中不难看出，查理二世在这六周里肯定是经历过很多九死一生的时刻，然而段落行文的重点在于描绘六周的事件发展，而不在于突出查理如何命悬一线，因此A项不准确。

B项：to suggest that Charles II’s supporters were badly prepared

译文：为了指出查理二世的支持者们没有做好什么准备

这个选项应该很好排除，其迷惑性甚至不如A项强，因为所有这些事件的起因发展显然都并不是围绕着“支持者们准备程度如何”来展开的。

D项：to argue that certain aspects are not as well known as they should be

译文：为了论证有一些故事的方面并不像它们原本应该的那样为人们所熟知

这个选项差不多算是“凭空出世”，在原文中没有任何对应，考生应该可以轻而易举地排除。

questions.prompt: What point does the reviewer make about Charles II in the fourth paragraph?

options.text: He chose to celebrate what was essentially a defeat.
He misunderstood the motives of his opponents.
He aimed to restore people's faith in the monarchy.
He was driven by a desire to be popular.

questions.explanation:
从第四段开始，书评人开始更多地脱离书里的讲述内容而更自由地发表了自己的看法。段落的前半部分先是分析了查理之所以失败的背后深层原因，然后开始跟进指出：查理本人事后竟然如此爱谈这段经历，十分有趣。紧接着，段中还给出了若干事例来展现查理是如何纪念这段人生插曲的，最后在结尾处发出了评论人的总结点评：很少能有其他国王会如此兴趣高涨地记录自己人生中的低谷。从这样的段落行文线索可知，正确答案应为A项：He chose to celebrate what was essentially a defeat.（他选择大肆颂扬一件本质上是场失败的事。）

本题的作答并不困难，部分原因是另外三个选项在第四段里基本没有可以对应之处，考生可轻松排除。

B项：He misunderstood the motives of his opponents.

译文：他误解了自己反对者们的动机。

C项：He aimed to restore people’s faith in the monarchy.

译文：他意在重塑人民对于统治君主的信心。

D项：He was driven by a desire to be popular.

译文：他被广受欢迎这个欲望所驱使。

questions.prompt: What does the reviewer say about Charles Spencer in the fifth paragraph?

options.text: His decision to write the book comes as a surprise.
He takes an unbiased approach to the subject matter.
His descriptions of events would be better if they included more detail.
He chooses language that is suitable for a twenty-first-century audience.

questions.explanation:
本题的解题难度可能主要来自于考生对unbiased这个基础高频词汇的认知能力。因此，前文将这个单词放在了必背词汇名单里，希望还没掌握该词的考生将其牢记。看懂了这个单词，再对比段落意思，特别是段中第三句话的表述，即可得出答案应为B项：He takes an unbiased approach to the subject matter.（他对这个话题采用了不偏不倚的态度。）

A项：His decision to write the book comes as a surprise.

译文：他写这本书的决定令人意外。

这是一个完全在本段里没有被提及过的信息。如果对标判断题的出题逻辑，这就是一个妥妥的NOT GIVEN选项。

C项：His descriptions of events would be better if they included more detail.

译文：他对事件的描述如果包含更多细节的话就会更好。

虽然在本段里并没有提到“描写细节”这个方面，但通过前文的阅读，考生其实应当已经有了这样的认知：本书最大的优点之一便是细节翔实丰富，这与选项所说内容是完全抵触矛盾的。

D项：He chooses language that is suitable for a twenty-first-century audience.

译文：他选择了适合21世纪读者的语言。

这个选项之所以构成了一定的干扰性，是因为本段中确实点评了这本书所使用的语言风格，然而细看之后不难发现：书评人对作者的语言风格给好评是一回事，至于这种语言风格是否适合21世纪的读者则是另一回事，后者并没有在段中被提及。

questions.prompt: When the reviewer says the book ‘doesn't quite hit the mark’, she is making the point that

options.text: it overlooks the impact of events on ordinary people.
it lacks an analysis of prevalent views on monarchy.
it omits any references to the deceit practised by Charles II during his time in hiding.
it fails to address whether Charles II's experiences had a lasting influence on him.

questions.explanation:
题干中的引号意味着引用的这部分内容是在段落中原词重现的，而这部分文字位于段落的中间位置，以this开头指代前文。不过，考生却无法通过只看This句的上一句来得出答案，而是还要参考再之前的几句话。这样看来，不如从一开始就抱定“平行阅读”的原则，直接从该段第一句开始读起，也并不吃亏。本段前半部分提出来的问题，正是围绕着“这六周的经历对查理产生的影响”来思考和假设的，考生完成这部分的准确理解后即不难锁定答案为D项：it fails to address whether Charles II’s experiences had a lasting influence on him.（它没能探讨查理二世的这段经历是否对他有着持续深远的影响。）

A项：it overlooks the impact of events on ordinary people.

译文：它忽略了这些事件对于普通人所产生的影响。

本项基本不存在什么迷惑性，因为全段乃至全文其实也不曾提及过“普通人”在这些事件中所受的影响。

B项：it lacks an analysis of prevalent views on monarchy.

译文：它缺乏对当时看待君主制的普遍观点的分析。

与A项类似，这个选项其实也跟段落所表达的文意风马牛不相及。

C项：it omits any references to the deceit practised by Charles II during his time in hiding.

译文：它没有提及任何查理二世在藏身期间所使用的欺骗手段。

本段中简单提及了查理二世为躲避追捕而使用的一些trickery和subterfuge，因此选项意思与原文相左，不足以干扰到考生答题。

articleHtml:
To catch a king

Anna Keay reviews Charles Spencer’s book about the hunt for King Charles II
during the English Civil War of the seventeenth century


Charles Spencer’s latest book, To Catch a King, tells us the story of the hunt for King Charles II in the six weeks after his resounding defeat at the Battle of Worcester in September 1651. And what a story it is. After his father was executed by the Parliamentarians in 1649, the young Charles II sacrificed one of the very principles his father had died for and did a deal with the Scots, thereby accepting Presbyterianism* as the national religion in return for being crowned King of Scots. His arrival in Edinburgh prompted the English Parliamentary army to invade Scotland in a pre-emptive strike. This was followed by a Scottish invasion of England. The two sides finally faced one another at Worcester in the west of England in 1651. After being comprehensively defeated on the meadows outside the city by the Parliamentarian army, the 21-year-old king found himself the subject of a national manhunt, with a huge sum offered for his capture. Over the following six weeks he managed, through a series of heart-poundingly close escapes, to evade the Parliamentarians before seeking refuge in France. For the next nine years, the penniless and defeated Charles wandered around Europe with only a small group of loyal supporters.

Years later, after his restoration as king, the 50-year-old Charles II requested a meeting with the writer and diarist Samuel Pepys. His intention when asking Pepys to commit his story to paper was to ensure that this most extraordinary episode was never forgotten. Over two three-hour sittings, the king related to him in great detail his personal recollections of the six weeks he had spent as a fugitive. As the king and secretary settled down (a scene that is surely a gift for a future scriptwriter), Charles commenced his story: ‘After the battle was so absolutely lost as to be beyond hope of recovery, I began to think of the best way of saving myself.’ 

One of the joys of Spencer’s book, a result not least of its use of Charles II’s own narrative as well as those of his supporters, is just how close the reader gets to the action. The day-byday retelling of the fugitives’ doings provides delicious details: the cutting of the king’s long hair with agricultural shears, the use of walnut leaves to dye his pale skin, and the day Charles spent lying on a branch of the great oak tree in Boscobel Wood as the Parliamentary soldiers scoured the forest floor below. Spencer draws out both the humour – such as the preposterous refusal of Charles’s friend Henry Wilmot to adopt disguise on the grounds that it was beneath his dignity – and the emotional tension when the secret of the king’s presence was cautiously revealed to his supporters. 

Charles’s adventures after losing the Battle of Worcester hide the uncomfortable truth that whilst almost everyone in England had been appalled by the execution of his father, they had not welcomed the arrival of his son with the Scots army, but had instead firmly bolted their doors. This was partly because he rode at the head of what looked like a foreign invasion force and partly because, after almost a decade of civil war, people were desperate to avoid it beginning again. This makes it all the more interesting that Charles II himself loved the story so much ever after. As well as retelling it to anyone who would listen, causing eyerolling among courtiers, he set in train a series of initiatives to memorialise it. There was to be a new order of chivalry, the Knights of the Royal Oak. A series of enormous oil paintings depicting the episode were produced, including a two-metre-wide canvas of Boscobel Wood and a set of six similarly enormous paintings of the king on the run. In 1660, Charles II commissioned the artist John Michael Wright to paint a flying squadron of cherubs* carrying an oak tree to the heavens on the ceiling of his bedchamber. It is hard to imagine many other kings marking the lowest point in their life so enthusiastically, or indeed pulling off such an escape in the first place. 

Charles Spencer is the perfect person to pass the story on to a new generation. His pacey, readable prose steers deftly clear of modern idioms and elegantly brings to life the details of the great tale. He has even-handed sympathy for both the fugitive king and the fierce republican regime that hunted him, and he succeeds in his desire to explore far more of the background of the story than previous books on the subject have done. Indeed, the opening third of the book is about how Charles II found himself at Worcester in the first place, which for some will be reason alone to read To Catch a King. 

The tantalising question left, in the end, is that of what it all meant. Would Charles II have been a different king had these six weeks never happened? The days and nights spent in hiding must have affected him in some way. Did the need to assume disguises, to survive on wit and charm alone, to use trickery and subterfuge to escape from tight corners help form him? This is the one area where the book doesn’t quite hit the mark. Instead its depiction of Charles II in his final years as an ineffective, pleasure-loving monarch doesn’t do justice to the man (neither is it accurate), or to the complexity of his character. But this one niggle aside, To Catch a King is an excellent read, and those who come to it knowing little of the famous tale will find they have a treat in store. 

* cherub: an image of angelic children used in paintings
